To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the number of stressors experienced during pregnancy is a significant predictor of birth outcomes when moderated by Medicaid.

(a) the more stressors a pregnant woman experiences, the more likely it is that her child will be small for gestational, (b) Medicaid status predicts problematic birth outcomes, but not small or large for age, (c) African-American women who are younger are at greater risk of having an infant who is born too small, and (d) the more stress a pregnant woman experiences the more likely it becomes that she will have an infant who is too small or too large.

the number of maternal stressors was only predictive of small for gestational weight when moderated by income, Medicaid status was a predictor of problematic birth and pre-term birth, and the relationship between race and adverse birth outcomes was moderated by age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of prenatal stress and the moderating effects of race and low income in a representative sample of the population in Tennessee.
the interplay of stressors, race, and low income in predicting adverse birth outcomes.
the effects of stress and low income on the birth outcomes of African-Americans and individuals from lower socioeconomic status.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
race is an important factor, as is age, in determining birth outcomes, and the effects of low income and race are moderated by the presence of other stressors.
the number of stressors a mother experiences during pregnancy does not have a direct effect on birth outcomes, but that it may be a predictor when moderated by other factors, such as Medicaid status.
race and low income are not independent factors that predict birth outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the number of stressors is not an independent predictor of adverse birth outcomes, but that low income and being African-American are risk factors for adverse birth outcomes, especially for young mothers.
low income and stressors during pregnancy are significant predictors of birth outcomes.
the stress of being poor is a more significant factor than race in determining the likelihood of a problematic birth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
race is an important predictor of birth outcomes and that the relationship between race and adverse birth outcomes varies with age.
low income and African American race are risk factors for adverse birth outcomes and these risk factors are interrelated.
race and low income are not the only factors to consider when assessing risk for birth complications.
